SECTION 1 — INTRODUCTION: RIGID BODIES AND TYPES OF MOTION

1.1 What is a Rigid Body?

note

Definition A is a body with a perfectly definite and unchanging shape. The distances between all pairs of particles remain constant, regardless of the forces acting.

No real body is truly rigid; deformations exist but are often negligible (e.g., a steel beam, a , a wheel of a vehicle).

1.2 Types of Motion of a Rigid Body

TypeDescriptionExample
All particles have the same velocity at every instantBlock sliding down inclined plane
Body rotates about a fixed axis; particles move in circlesCeiling fan, Potter's wheel
Translation + Rotation combinedCylinder rolling down an incline
important

Key Principle In pure translation, every particle has the same velocity. In pure rotation about a fixed axis, every particle has the same ω.

Left: every particle of a purely translating body carries an identical velocity vector at any instant — the body's orientation never changes. Right: in pure rotation, every particle shares the same angular velocity ω, but because v=ωr, a point farther from the axis (like P2​) has a larger linear speed than one closer in (P1​), even though both "keep pace" angularly.

1.3 Rotation About a Fixed Axis

  • Every particle moves in a circle lying in a plane perpendicular to the fixed axis, with its centre on the axis.

  • A particle at perpendicular distance r from the axis traces a circle of radius r.

  • Particles on the axis have r = 0, so v = ωr = 0 → they remain stationary.

  • The axis of a spinning top is not fixed (it precesses) — our chapter mainly deals with .

1.4 Interactive — Why Different Points Have Different Speeds

The TikZ figure above is a snapshot; this graph is the mechanism. Five points sit at different radii on the same rotating disc (same ω for all of them, exactly as the Key Principle box states). Drag ω and watch every arrow's length scale — linearly with r, never with anything else.

Every arrow points along its own tangent — none of them parallel — but the ratio ∣Vi​∣/ri​ is the same number (=ω) for all five points, every single frame. That ratio being constant is the content of Eq. (6.19), vi​=ωri​.

SECTION 2 — CENTRE OF MASS (COM)

2.1 What Is the Centre of Mass?

note

Definition The (COM) is that single point which moves in exactly the same way a single particle — carrying the total mass of the system — would move if the same external force were applied to it.

The COM is a bookkeeping device: instead of tracking every particle of a possibly-huge system individually, track this one point, and you have completely captured the system's translational behaviour. Sections 2 and 3 make this idea precise; Section 3 in particular shows why this definition is dynamically useful, not just geometrically convenient.

2.2 Two-Particle System — Derivation

Consider two particles of masses m1​ and m2​ with position vectors r1​ and r2​ from some origin O. Their is the point C, with position vector Rcm​:

Rcm​=m1​+m2​m1​r1​+m2​r2​​

Restricting motion to the x-axis (as is conventional for the scalar derivation) and writing r1​→x1​, r2​→x2​, Rcm​→xcm​:

Step 1 — the weighted-sum relation:

(m1​+m2​)xcm​=m1​x1​+m2​x2​

Step 2 — solve for xcm​:

xcm​=m1​+m2​m1​x1​+m2​x2​​​...(6.1)

The same steps along y give ycm​=m1​+m2​m1​y1​+m2​y2​​.

Step 3 — special case, equal masses (m1​=m2​=m):

xcm​=2mmx1​+mx2​​=2x1​+x2​​

For equal masses, the COM lies exactly midway between them — this falls out of the general weighted-average result; it is not a separate rule to memorise.

note

Reading xcm​X in Eq. (6.1) is the mass-weighted mean of x1​ and x2​ — it is pulled toward whichever particle is heavier, exactly like a weighted average in statistics.

2.3 General Case — n Particles

X=M∑mi​xi​​,Y=M∑mi​yi​​,Z=M∑mi​zi​​​...(6.4a–c)

where M=∑mi​ is the total mass.

In vector form:

R=M∑mi​ri​​​...(6.4d)

note

Origin Choice If the origin is chosen at the , then ∑mi​ri​=0.

2.4 Continuous Mass Distribution

X=M1​∫xdm,Y=M1​∫ydm,Z=M1​∫zdm...(6.5a)

For uniform, symmetric bodies: The coincides with the geometric centre — by symmetry, for every element dm at r, there is an element dm at −r, so the integrals vanish.

SECTION 3 — MOTION OF THE CENTRE OF MASS

3.1 Derivation: The Centre of Mass Obeys Newton's Second Law

This is the result that makes the more than a geometric curiosity — it shows that a system's COM moves exactly like a single particle of mass M under the net external force, no matter how complicated the internal motion is.

Start from Eq. (6.4d): MR=∑mi​ri​.

Step 1 — differentiate once (masses are constant in time):

MdtdR​=∑mi​dtdri​​

MV=∑mi​vi​=m1​v1​+m2​v2​+…​...(6.8)

Here V=dR/dt is the velocity of the COM.

Step 2 — differentiate again:

MdtdV​=∑mi​dtdvi​​

MA=∑mi​ai​=m1​a1​+m2​a2​+…​...(6.9)

Here A=dV/dt is the acceleration of the COM.

Step 3 — bring in Newton's second law for each particle. The force on particle i is Fi​=mi​ai​ (this Fi​ already includes both external and internal forces on that particle), so:

MA=F1​+F2​+⋯+Fn​...(6.10)

Step 4 — internal forces cancel. Every internal force (particle j on particle i) is matched by an equal-and-opposite reaction (particle i on particle j), by Newton's third law. Summed over the whole system, these pairs cancel exactly, leaving only the external forces:

MA=Fext​​...(6.11)

important

The Big Idea The centre of mass of a moves as if all the mass of the system were concentrated at the COM, and all the external forces were applied at that point — regardless of whether the system is rigid, deforming, exploding, or has any internal motion whatsoever. To find the motion of the COM, you never need to know the internal forces.

A shell following a parabolic trajectory explodes mid-air into fragments. The forces of the explosion are internal — they contribute nothing to Eq. (6.11). The only external force throughout is gravity, unchanged by the explosion. So the COM of the fragments continues along the exact same parabolic path the unexploded shell would have followed — even as individual fragments fly off in wildly different directions.

3.2 Consequence — Radioactive Decay and Binary Stars

  • Radioactive decay: A radium nucleus at rest decays into a radon nucleus and an alpha particle. Since there's no external force, the stays at rest — the two products must fly apart back-to-back, in exactly opposite directions.

  • Binary stars: With no external force, the COM of a double-star system moves like a free particle (uniform velocity, or rest). In the COM frame, the two stars orbit the (stationary) COM in circles, always diametrically opposite each other.

tip

Problem-Solving Technique Separating a system's motion into () translation of the COM and (ii) motion relative to the COM is one of the most powerful techniques in mechanics — it lets you analyse the "boring" overall drift and the "interesting" internal dynamics independently.

SECTION 4 — VECTOR PRODUCT OF TWO VECTORS

4.1 Why We Need It

Two of the most important rotational quantities — and — are defined using a new kind of vector multiplication: the .

4.2 Definition

note

Definition The (cross product) of a and b is a vector c=a×b such that:

  1. Magnitude: ∣c∣=absinθ, where θ is the angle between a and b.

  2. Direction: c is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b.

  3. Sense: given by the right-hand screw rule — curl the fingers of the right hand from a to b (through the smaller angle); the thumb points along c.

The cross product c points straight out of the plane containing a and b — here, "out of the page," toward the viewer.

4.3 Key Properties

PropertyStatement
Not commutativea×b=−b×a
Not associative in generalOrder and grouping matter
Distributivea×(b+c)=a×b+a×c
Self a×a=0 (since sin0∘=0)
Behaviour under reflectiona×b does not change sign under reflection (unlike ordinary/"polar" vectors)

4.4 Unit Vector Rules

^×^=^​×^​=k^×k^=0

^×^​=k^,^​×k^=^,k^×^=^​

tip

Cyclic Order Trick If ^,^​,k^ occur in cyclic order (^→^​→k^→^→…), the product is positive. Reverse the order and it's negative: ^​×^=−k^, k^×^​=−^, ^×k^=−^​.

4.5 Component (Determinant) Form

a×b=​^ax​bx​​^​ay​by​​k^az​bz​​​=(ay​bz​−az​by​)^+(az​bx​−ax​bz​)^​+(ax​by​−ay​bx​)k^

SECTION 5 — ANGULAR VELOCITY AND ITS RELATION WITH LINEAR VELOCITY

5.1 Angular Velocity — Definition

note

Definition ω is the time rate of change of : ω=limΔt→0​ΔtΔθ​=dtdθ​SI unit: rad s⁻¹. Dimensional formula:[T−1].

For a particle at perpendicular distance ri​ from a fixed axis:

vi​=ωri​...(6.19)

The same ω applies to every particle of the body — this is why we speak of "the angular velocity of the body" as a single number, even though different particles have different linear speeds.

Vector form, valid even for rotation about one fixed point (not just a fixed axis):

v=ω×r​...(6.20)

Since ω lies along OC (the axis) and r=OC+CP, and ω×OC=0 (parallel vectors), we get ω×r=ω×CP — a vector of magnitude ωr⊥​, tangential to the circle at P. This confirms ∣v∣=ωr⊥​, matching Eq. (6.19).

tip

The Four Rotational Cross-Products Every core relation in this chapter is a pairing an angular quantity with a position (or momentum) vector. Keep these four together:

RelationGives youRotational analogue of
v=ω×rlinear velocity—
at​=α×rtangential acceleration—
L=r×plinear momentum p=mv
τ=r×Fforce F

5.2 Angular Acceleration

note

Definition α=dtdω​,scalar form (fixed axis): α=dtdω​...(6.21), (6.22)SI unit: rad s⁻². Dimensional formula:[T−2].

For fixed-axis rotation, ω's direction never changes — only its magnitude can — so α is also fixed in direction, and the vector equation collapses to the scalar one above.

5.3 Tangential and Centripetal Acceleration in Rotation

A particle undergoing circular motion in a rotating has, in general, two perpendicular components of acceleration:

at​=α×r,∣at​∣=αr⊥​​(tangential — speeds it up/slows it down along the circle)

ac​=ω2r⊥​=r⊥​v2​​(centripetal — always toward the axis, changes direction only)

How at​ and ac​ actually scale — plotted, not just stated: at​=αr is a straight line against ω (it doesn't even depend on ω!), while ac​=ω2r is a parabola. This is easy to state and easy to forget — plotting both against the same axis makes the quadratic growth of ac​ impossible to un-see.

Slide the angular-speed slider w to the right: the point on the flat line ar barely moves, but the point on x2r shoots upward — double w and ac​ quadruples, not doubles.

warning

Common Confusion at​=αr⊥​ is only the tangential part. It vanishes when ω is constant (α=0) — but the particle is still accelerating centripetally, ac​=ω2r⊥​=0, as long as it keeps moving in a circle at all. "No " does not mean "no acceleration."

SECTION 6 — TORQUE AND ANGULAR MOMENTUM

6.1 Moment of Force (Torque)

note

Definition The (moment of force) of F acting at point P (position vector r from origin O) is: τ=r×F​...(6.23)SI unit: N m. Dimensional formula:[ML2T−2] — dimensionally identical to energy, but torque is a vector, energy is a scalar; never equate them physically.

τ=rFsinθ=rF⊥​=r⊥​F...(6.24a–c)

Torque vanishes if r=0, F=0, or if the line of action of F passes through the origin (θ=0° or 180°).

If F is reversed, τ reverses. If both r and F are reversed, τ is unchanged (two sign flips cancel).

Interactive — the sinθ dependence, isolated: hold r and F fixed and sweep only the angle between them. This is the reason pushing a door near the hinge barely turns it (small effective moment) while the same push at the door's outer edge, applied perpendicular, is maximally effective — it's not really about distance from the hinge at all, it's about sinθ.

Desmos variableMeaning
r,Ffixed magnitudes of r and F
qangle between them — drag this one
y(x)rFsinx, plotted as a function of the angle

Drag the angle slider q from 0 to π: the torque starts at zero, peaks exactly at q=π/2 (force perpendicular to r — the most effective angle possible), then falls back to zero at q=π (force now anti-parallel to r, along the same line — no turning effect at all, matching the "vanishes if the line of action passes through the origin" rule above).

6.2 Angular Momentum of a Particle

note

Definition L=r×p​...(6.25a)SI unit: kg m² s⁻¹ (= J s). Dimensional formula:[ML2T−1].

L=rpsinθ=rp⊥​=r⊥​p...(6.26a,b)

Rate of change of equals — derived by differentiating L=r×p:

dtdL​=dtdr​×p+r×dtdp​=v×mv+r×F=0+r×F

dtdL​=τ​...(6.27)

(v×mv=0 because the of any vector with itself — or a scalar multiple of itself — vanishes.) This is the exact rotational analogue of F=dp/dt.

Interactive 3D — L=r×p for a particle going in a circle: this is the object Eq. (6.25a) actually is — not a formula, a vector. Here a particle of mass m moves on a circle of radius R in the xy-plane with angular speed ω; r and p both sweep around together, yet their cross product L never changes — same direction (+z), same magnitude, every instant. That's Section 11's whole "L=Iω= constant" idea, seen a chapter early, from first principles.

Drag q through a full revolution: r and p​ both rotate in the xy-plane, but L stands perfectly still, pointing along +z, with its magnitude fixed at mwR2 throughout — exactly the invariance Example 6.6 proves algebraically for a straight-line particle, now shown for a circular one.

6.3 Torque and Angular Momentum for a System of Particles

L=∑i​li​=∑i​ri​×pi​...(6.25b)

Differentiating, and using dli​/dt=τi​ for each particle:

dtdL​=∑i​τi​=∑i​ri​×Fi​...(6.28a)

Each Fi​ splits into an external part and an internal part, so the total splits the same way:

τ=τext​+τint​

warning

Why τint​=0 needs TWO assumptions, not one It's tempting to say "internal torques cancel by Newton's third law" and stop there — that's incomplete. Newton's third law only guarantees that the force pair between any two particles is equal and opposite; by itself, that does not force their torques to cancel. Cancellation additionally requires the internal forces to act along the line joining the two particles (.e., they are central forces). Only with both Newton's third law and collinearity does every action–reaction pair contribute zero net torque about any point.

With both assumptions in place, τint​=0, giving:

dtdL​=τext​​...(6.28b)

Conservation of : if τext​=0, then L=constant — Eq. (6.29a), the rotational analogue of momentum conservation.

SECTION 7 — EQUILIBRIUM OF A RIGID BODY

7.1 Conditions for Mechanical Equilibrium

A is in equilibrium when it has neither linear nor :

∑Fi​=0​(Translational equilibrium) ...(6.30a)

∑τi​=0​(Rotational equilibrium) ...(6.30b)

note

The condition is independent of the choice of origin (provided also holds) — so you're always free to take moments about whichever point makes the algebra simplest.

7.2 Partial Equilibrium

A body can satisfy one condition without the other:

  • only, NOT translational: two equal, parallel forces in the same direction at the two ends of a rod. Moments about the midpoint cancel (equal and opposite in sense), but net force =2F=0.

  • only, NOT rotational: reverse one of those forces — now net force =0, but the two forces form a , so moments add up rather than cancel, and the rod undergoes with no translation.

7.3 Couple

note

Definition A is a pair of forces of equal magnitude acting in opposite directions with different (parallel) lines of action. A couple produces rotation without translation.

of a couple =AB×F, and this is independent of the origin chosen to compute moments — a distinguishing feature of couples (proved by taking moments of F at B and −F at A about an arbitrary point and simplifying; the origin-dependent terms cancel).

Examples: turning a bottle cap with your fingers, a compass needle in the Earth's magnetic field (equal and opposite forces on the N and S poles).

d1​F1​=d2​F2​​...(6.32a)

7.5 Centre of Gravity (CG)

note

Definition The (CG) is the point where the total gravitational on the body is zero.

∑τg​=∑ri​×mi​g=0...(6.33)

Since g is the same for every particle in an ordinary-sized body, it factors out of the sum — leaving ∑mi​ri​=0, exactly the condition that defines the . So:

important

CG coincides with COM for any body small enough that g doesn't vary across it. For a body so large that g varies from one part to another (astronomically large structures), CG and COM would differ — but this never arises in this course.

Finding CG of an irregular body experimentally: suspend it from a point A; the vertical line through A passes through the CG. Suspend it again from a different point B; the intersection of the two vertical lines locates the CG exactly.

SECTION 8 — MOMENT OF INERTIA

8.1 Definition

The (MI) of a about an axis:

I=i∑​mi​ri2​​...(6.34)

where ri​ is the perpendicular distance of the ith particle from the axis.

  • SI unit: kg m²; Dimensional formula: [ML2]

  • Depends on: mass, distribution of mass about the axis, and position/orientation of axis.

  • Unlike mass, I is NOT a fixed property of the body — it changes with the axis chosen. The same disc has a different I about its central axis than about its diameter.

Notice how heavily I weights distance, not just mass — a small mass far from the axis can contribute more to I than a large mass close to it, because of the ri2​ factor.

Interactive — same M, same R, wildly different I: four bodies, identical total mass M and identical outer radius R, but with that mass distributed differently relative to the axis. The bar heights below are exactly the coefficients in Table 6.1 (§8.4) — this is why the table has different numbers for shapes that look similarly sized.

Desmos variableMeaning
M,Rshared mass and radius — drag either
Ipoint​all mass at radius R (point mass / thin ring)
Idisc​mass spread uniformly out to R (disc)
Isphere​mass spread through the whole volume (solid sphere)

Drag R upward: all three bars grow, but Ipoint​ always grows fastest, because every last bit of its mass sits at the maximum possible distance R; Isphere​ always trails, because most of a sphere's mass sits well inside its outer radius, closer to the axis than R.

8.2 Kinetic Energy of Rotation

Krot​=21​Iω2​...(6.35)

Derivation: each particle moves in a circle with speed vi​=ri​ω, so its KE is 21​mi​vi2​=21​mi​ri2​ω2. Summing over all particles, with ω common to every one of them:

K=∑i​21​mi​ri2​ω2=21​ω2∑i​mi​ri2​=21​Iω2

Compare with translational KE K=21​mv2 → I is the rotational analogue of mass m; ω is the analogue of v.

8.3 Radius of Gyration k ⭐⭐

note

Definition The k about a given axis is the distance from the axis at which the entire mass of the body, if concentrated as a single point, would produce the same as the actual body. Equivalently, k is the RMS (root-mean-square) value of the distances of all the particles from the axis: k=nr12​+r22​+⋯+rn2​​​SI unit: m. Dimensional formula:[L].

Derivation of I=Mk2: Suppose (for a clean derivation) that the body is made of n identical particles, each of mass m, so M=mn.

Step 1: I=∑i​mi​ri2​=m∑i​ri2​(mass m is common, pull it out)

Step 2 — multiply and divide by n: I=(mn)(n∑i​ri2​​)

Step 3 — identify the two factors: mn=M (total mass), and n∑ri2​​=k2 (mean-square distance, by definition above):

I=Mk2⟹k=I/M​​

8.5 Two Special Cases (NCERT derivations)

(a) Thin ring (radius R, mass M), rotating about its own central axis

All mass is at the same distance R from the axis: K=21​Mv2=21​M(Rω)2=21​(MR2)ω2. Comparing with K=21​Iω2: Iring​=MR2.

(b) Rod of negligible mass, length l, with point masses M/2 at each end, rotating about a perpendicular axis through the centre

I=2M​(2l​)2+2M​(2l​)2=4Ml2​

8.6 Parallel Axis Theorem ⭐⭐⭐

note

Statement The of a body about any axis equals the moment of inertia about a parallel axis through the , plus Md2, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two axes: I′=Icm​+Md2​

Interactive — watch I′ grow as the axis moves away: slide d from 0 (back at the centre) outward, and watch I′=Icm​+Md2 trace out a parabola in d — never a straight line. This is the same "quadratic, not linear" lesson as §5.3's ac​=ω2r graph, showing up again in a completely different part of the chapter.

Because it's Md2 and not Md, doubling d quadruples the extra term — moving an axis just a little further out costs far more than intuition suggests.

8.7 Perpendicular Axis Theorem ⭐⭐⭐

note

Statement For a planar (laminar) body only, the about an axis perpendicular to its plane equals the sum of the moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes in its own plane, all three axes intersecting at one point: Iz​=Ix​+Iy​​,Ix​=∑mi​xi2​,Iy​=∑mi​yi2​,Iz​=∑mi​zi2​

warning

Critical Restriction The applies only to flat, two-dimensional (planar/laminar) bodies — rings, discs, plane laminas. It does not apply to three-dimensional solids like a solid sphere or a solid cylinder, because those bodies have mass genuinely spread along the z-direction too, not confined to the xy-plane.

8.8 Flywheel — Practical Application

A is a disc with large I used in steam engines and automobiles. Because of its large I, it resists sudden changes in angular speed → smooth, jerk-free motion, even as the driving fluctuates.

SECTION 9 — KINEMATICS OF ROTATIONAL MOTION ABOUT A FIXED AXIS

9.1 Equations of Motion (Uniform Angular Acceleration)

Exact analogues of the linear kinematic equations:

LinearRotational
v=v0​+atω=ω0​+αt ...(6.36)
x=x0​+v0​t+21​at2θ=θ0​+ω0​t+21​αt2 ...(6.37)

These apply only when α is constant (uniform).

9.2 Derivation of Eq. (6.36)

Since α=dω/dt= constant, integrating: ω=αt+c. At t=0, ω=ω0​⇒c=ω0​.

Therefore ω=ω0​+αt ✓

Integrating again: θ=θ0​+ω0​t+21​αt2 ✓

tip

Quick Convert: rpm → rad/s If N is the speed in revolutions per minute (rpm): ω=2π(60N​)=30πN​ rad/s This shortcut saves a step in almost every rotational-kinematics numerical.

SECTION 10 — DYNAMICS OF ROTATIONAL MOTION ABOUT A FIXED AXIS

10.1 Torque and Angular Acceleration

From the work-energy route (or directly from Newton's 2nd Law applied to rotation):

τ=Iα​...(6.41)

This is the exact rotational analogue of F=ma: produces , exactly as force produces linear acceleration, with I playing the role of inertia.

Interactive — same torque, different I, very different response: exactly the same shape of relationship as §11.2's ω=L/I hyperbola, but now for dynamics rather than conservation. Hold τ fixed and drag I: a small I (a light disc) snaps into fast rotation; a large I (a heavy ) barely budges under the same push. This is the entire reason a flywheel resists jerky speed changes (§8.8) — not a separate fact, but this exact curve.

Drag I down toward 0.5 and the angular acceleration T/I spikes; drag it up toward 8 and it barely registers — the same fixed torque, wildly different outcomes, purely because of how the mass is distributed.

matching the linear forms dW=Fds and P=Fv.

SECTION 11 — ANGULAR MOMENTUM IN CASE OF ROTATION ABOUT A FIXED AXIS

11.1 Setting Up: Lz​=Iω

For a symmetric about its (an axis of symmetry — true for every body in Table 6.1), the component of along the axis works out to:

L=Iω​...(6.42d)

Differentiating, and using dL/dt=τext​ (Eq. 6.28b) restricted to the fixed-axis component:

dtd​(Iω)=τext​

If I itself doesn't change with time, this reduces straight back to τ=Iα (Eq. 6.41) — consistent with Section 10.

warning

L and ω are not always parallel In general, for a body not symmetric about its rotation axis, L=Lz​ and L does not lie along the axis at all. The simple relation L=Iω (as vectors) is a special-case convenience for symmetric bodies — the only kind this course deals with — not a universal law.

11.2 Conservation of Angular Momentum

If I is allowed to change (mass redistributes relative to the axis) but τext​=0:

Lz​=Iω=constant​...(6.44)

So if I decreases, ω must increase to keep Iω fixed, and vice versa — this is the single most powerful idea in the chapter for solving "sudden change in shape/configuration" problems.

Turn this into a dial you can actually drag: with L held fixed, ω and I trace out the hyperbola ω=L/I below — pull Inow​ toward zero (arms tucked in tight) and watch ωnow​ shoot upward, exactly the "arms in → spin faster" effect in the panel above, now with numbers attached.

Watch K=L2/(2I) climb as you drag I down — this is the "kinetic energy increases" claim below, made concrete: halving I doesn't just double K, it quadruples it, because K∝1/I while ω∝1/I too.

A skater (or a person on a frictionless swivel chair) pulls their arms in: I decreases sharply, so ω increases to conserve L=Iω. Pulling arms back out reverses the effect. The kinetic energy K=21​Iω2=21​Lω actually increases when arms are pulled in (since ω increases while L stays fixed) — that extra energy comes from the muscular work done pulling the arms inward against the effective outward pull, not from nowhere.

11.3 Earth Shrinks: Change in Day Length

⚡ POINTS TO PONDER (High-Yield for Exams)

  1. COM ≠ geometric centre for non-uniform bodies. The COM is the mass-weighted average position; it coincides with the geometric centre only for uniform symmetric bodies.

  2. COM can lie outside the body. For a ring, the COM is at the centre — in empty space. Similarly for a hollow sphere, L-shaped body, etc.

  3. Internal forces don't affect COM motion. An explosion in mid-air doesn't change the path of the COM — only external forces (gravity) determine COM motion. To find COM motion, you never need to know the internal forces at all.

  4. Torque and work: same dimensions, different quantities. Both [ML2T−2] = N m, but torque is a vector (cross product) and work is a scalar (dot product) — never equate them physically.

  5. A couple has zero net force but non-zero torque. You can have without , or vice versa — the two conditions are independent.

  6. Internal torques cancel only under two conditions together: Newton's third law (equal and opposite) and the forces being directed along the line joining the particles (collinear/central). Drop either assumption and the cancellation fails.

  7. The total torque on a system is origin-independent only if the net external force is zero — otherwise, changing your reference point changes the computed torque.

  8. Moment of inertia depends on the axis. The same cylinder has I=MR2/2 for its own axis but a different I for a diameter. Always specify the axis.

  9. works for any and any pair of parallel axes, and shows Icm​ is always the smallest possible moment of inertia among all parallel axes (since Md2≥0 only ever adds).

  10. applies ONLY to flat, planar (2-D) bodies — never apply it to a 3-D solid like a sphere or a solid cylinder, whose mass isn't confined to one plane.

  11. CG coincides with COM only if g doesn't vary across the body — always true in this course, but not true for astronomically large bodies.

  12. Skater analogy: L=Iω= constant. Pulling arms in reduces I → ω increases. The kinetic energy increases (K=L2/2I) — the extra energy comes from muscular work done while pulling in the arms, not from nowhere.

  13. Rolling (for reference, next chapter): Total KE =21​Mv2+21​Iω2. For rolling without slipping: v=Rω.

  14. Perpendicular distance in torque: τ=r⊥​F=rF⊥​. Both interpretations give the same result — use whichever is more convenient for the given geometry.

  15. Angular momentum of a linearly moving particle: A particle moving in a straight line has non-zero angular momentum about any point NOT on its line of motion — and this angular momentum stays constant, since there is no torque on a free particle (Example 6.6).

  16. L and ω are parallel only when the rotation axis is a symmetry axis of the body — this is why L=Iω works cleanly for every body in Table 6.1, but is not a universally true vector relation.

🧭 PROBLEM-SOLVING STRATEGY

Type A — Centre of Mass problems

  1. Identify whether the system is discrete particles or a continuous body.

  2. For discrete systems: set up a coordinate origin, list every (mi​,xi​,yi​), and apply X=∑mi​xi​/M.

  3. For continuous, uniform, symmetric bodies: COM = geometric centre — skip the integral entirely.

  4. For composite shapes (like an L-lamina): split into simple sub-shapes, treat each sub-shape's mass as concentrated at its own COM, then apply the discrete formula to those points.

Type B — Equilibrium problems (levers, ladders, beams)

  1. Draw a clean free-body diagram; mark every force with its point of application.

  2. Write the translational equilibrium equations (∑Fx​=0, ∑Fy​=0).

  3. Choose a smart pivot point for moments — usually the point where the most unknown forces act, so they drop out of the torque equation.

  4. Write the rotational equilibrium equation (∑τ=0) about that pivot.

  5. Solve the resulting system (usually 2–3 equations) simultaneously.

Type C — Moment of Inertia and Axis Theorem problems

  1. Identify the body's shape and check Table 6.1 for I about the "natural" axis (through the centre).

  2. If the target axis is parallel to that natural axis → Parallel Axis Theorem, I′=Icm​+Md2.

  3. If the body is planar and you need I about an axis perpendicular to its plane, or want to split Iz​ into in-plane components → Perpendicular Axis Theorem, Iz​=Ix​+Iy​.

  4. For composite bodies, find I of each piece about the same axis (using the theorems as needed) and add.

Type D — Combined Rotational Kinematics + Dynamics

  1. From the given information, find τ (from forces) and I (from geometry/mass) separately.

  2. Get α=τ/I.

  3. Feed α into the standard kinematic equations (6.36)–(6.38) to find ω, θ, or t as needed.

  4. Cross-check energy: work done by external torque should equal the kinetic energy gained (if no friction).

Type E — Angular Momentum Conservation problems

  1. Confirm τext​=0 about the axis in question (internal reconfiguration, no outside twist).

  2. Write I1​ω1​=I2​ω2​.

  3. Compute I1​ and I2​ from the geometry before and after the change.

  4. Solve for the unknown ω — and if asked about energy, remember K is generally not conserved even though L is (any change in K is accounted for by real work done in changing the configuration).

Example 6.2 — Centre of mass of a triangular lamina (uniform)

Example 6.2 — Centre of mass of a triangular lamina (uniform)

Reveal answer

Subdivide the lamina△LMNinto narrow strips parallel to the baseMN. By symmetry, each strip's own centre of mass sits at its midpoint. Joining the midpoints of every strip traces out the medianLP— so the COM of thewholetriangle must lie somewhere onLP.

The same argument applied to strips parallel to the other two sides shows the COM also lies on mediansMQandNR.

A point that lies on all three medians simultaneously must be theirpoint of concurrence— thecentroidG. Hence, for a uniform triangular lamina, theCOM coincides with the centroid, regardless of the triangle's shape.

4.2 Definition

note

Definition The (cross product) of a and b is a vector c=a×b such that:

  1. Magnitude: ∣c∣=absinθ, where θ is the angle between a and b.

  2. Direction: c is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b.

  3. Sense: given by the right-hand screw rule — curl the fingers of the right hand from a to b (through the smaller angle); the thumb points along c.

The cross product c points straight out of the plane containing a and b — here, "out of the page," toward the viewer.

6.1 Moment of Force (Torque)

note

Definition The (moment of force) of F acting at point P (position vector r from origin O) is: τ=r×F​...(6.23)SI unit: N m. Dimensional formula:[ML2T−2] — dimensionally identical to energy, but torque is a vector, energy is a scalar; never equate them physically.

τ=rFsinθ=rF⊥​=r⊥​F...(6.24a–c)

Torque vanishes if r=0, F=0, or if the line of action of F passes through the origin (θ=0° or 180°).

If F is reversed, τ reverses. If both r and F are reversed, τ is unchanged (two sign flips cancel).

Interactive — the sinθ dependence, isolated: hold r and F fixed and sweep only the angle between them. This is the reason pushing a door near the hinge barely turns it (small effective moment) while the same push at the door's outer edge, applied perpendicular, is maximally effective — it's not really about distance from the hinge at all, it's about sinθ.

6.1 Moment of Force (Torque)

note

Definition The (moment of force) of F acting at point P (position vector r from origin O) is: τ=r×F​...(6.23)SI unit: N m. Dimensional formula:[ML2T−2] — dimensionally identical to energy, but torque is a vector, energy is a scalar; never equate them physically.

τ=rFsinθ=rF⊥​=r⊥​F...(6.24a–c)

Torque vanishes if r=0, F=0, or if the line of action of F passes through the origin (θ=0° or 180°).

If F is reversed, τ reverses. If both r and F are reversed, τ is unchanged (two sign flips cancel).

Interactive — the sinθ dependence, isolated: hold r and F fixed and sweep only the angle between them. This is the reason pushing a door near the hinge barely turns it (small effective moment) while the same push at the door's outer edge, applied perpendicular, is maximally effective — it's not really about distance from the hinge at all, it's about sinθ.

Desmos variableMeaning
r,Ffixed magnitudes of r and F
qangle between them — drag this one
y(x)rFsinx, plotted as a function of the angle

Drag the angle slider q from 0 to π: the torque starts at zero, peaks exactly at q=π/2 (force perpendicular to r — the most effective angle possible), then falls back to zero at q=π (force now anti-parallel to r, along the same line — no turning effect at all, matching the "vanishes if the line of action passes through the origin" rule above).

Example — Torque from a time-varying momentum

6.4

A particle sits at the fixed positionr=^+^​−k^while its momentum varies asp(t)=5t^+9t2^​−3k^. Find the torque on it as a function of time.

Reveal answer

Step 1 — findL(t)=r×p(t):^:(1)(−3)−(−1)(9t2)=9t2−3;^​:(−1)(5t)−(1)(−3)=3−5t;k^:(1)(9t2)−(1)(5t)=9t2−5t.

L(t)=(9t2−3)^+(3−5t)^​+(9t2−5t)k^

Step 2 — differentiate component-wise, usingτ=dL/dt:

τ(t)=18t^−5^​+(18t−5)k^​

This is a genuinely useful example because it showsτ=dL/dtbeing used the way it's actually tested — via differentiation of a time-dependentL, not justr×Fread off directly.

6.3 Torque and Angular Momentum for a System of Particles

L=∑i​li​=∑i​ri​×pi​...(6.25b)

Differentiating, and using dli​/dt=τi​ for each particle:

dtdL​=∑i​τi​=∑i​ri​×Fi​...(6.28a)

Each Fi​ splits into an external part and an internal part, so the total splits the same way:

τ=τext​+τint​

warning

Why τint​=0 needs TWO assumptions, not one It's tempting to say "internal torques cancel by Newton's third law" and stop there — that's incomplete. Newton's third law only guarantees that the force pair between any two particles is equal and opposite; by itself, that does not force their torques to cancel. Cancellation additionally requires the internal forces to act along the line joining the two particles (.e., they are central forces). Only with both Newton's third law and collinearity does every action–reaction pair contribute zero net torque about any point.

With both assumptions in place, τint​=0, giving:

dtdL​=τext​​...(6.28b)

Conservation of : if τext​=0, then L=constant — Eq. (6.29a), the rotational analogue of momentum conservation.

Worked application — Rod about one end

8.6

A uniform rod of massM, lengthLhasIcm​=ML2/12(axis through centre, perpendicular to rod). FindIabout aparallel axis through one end.

Reveal answer

Hered=L/2(perpendicular distance from centre to end):

Iend​=Icm​+Md2=12ML2​+M(2L​)2=12ML2​+4ML2​=3ML2​​

This is one of the most frequently tested single results in the whole chapter — memorise bothML2/12(centre) andML2/3(end), and know how they're related.

8.6 Parallel Axis Theorem ⭐⭐⭐

note

Statement The of a body about any axis equals the moment of inertia about a parallel axis through the , plus Md2, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two axes: I′=Icm​+Md2​

Interactive — watch I′ grow as the axis moves away: slide d from 0 (back at the centre) outward, and watch I′=Icm​+Md2 trace out a parabola in d — never a straight line. This is the same "quadratic, not linear" lesson as §5.3's ac​=ω2r graph, showing up again in a completely different part of the chapter.

Because it's Md2 and not Md, doubling d quadruples the extra term — moving an axis just a little further out costs far more than intuition suggests.

Worked application — Disc about a diameter, from the disc about its centre

8.7

A uniform disc hasIz​=MR2/2about the axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane (Table 6.1). By symmetry, the two in-plane diameters (any two mutually perpendicular ones) must haveequalmoments of inertia:Ix​=Iy​. By the perpendicular axis theorem:

Reveal answer

Iz​=Ix​+Iy​=2Ix​⇒Ix​=2Iz​​=2MR2/2​=4MR2​​

This exactly reproduces the "disc about diameter" row of Table 6.1 — confirming the theorem and showing how the table's own entries arenotindependent facts, but consequences of each other.

8.7 Perpendicular Axis Theorem ⭐⭐⭐

note

Statement For a planar (laminar) body only, the about an axis perpendicular to its plane equals the sum of the moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes in its own plane, all three axes intersecting at one point: Iz​=Ix​+Iy​​,Ix​=∑mi​xi2​,Iy​=∑mi​yi2​,Iz​=∑mi​zi2​

warning

Critical Restriction The applies only to flat, two-dimensional (planar/laminar) bodies — rings, discs, plane laminas. It does not apply to three-dimensional solids like a solid sphere or a solid cylinder, because those bodies have mass genuinely spread along the z-direction too, not confined to the xy-plane.

5.1 Angular Velocity — Definition

note

Definition ω is the time rate of change of : ω=limΔt→0​ΔtΔθ​=dtdθ​SI unit: rad s⁻¹. Dimensional formula:[T−1].

For a particle at perpendicular distance ri​ from a fixed axis:

vi​=ωri​...(6.19)

The same ω applies to every particle of the body — this is why we speak of "the angular velocity of the body" as a single number, even though different particles have different linear speeds.

Vector form, valid even for rotation about one fixed point (not just a fixed axis):

v=ω×r​...(6.20)

Since ω lies along OC (the axis) and r=OC+CP, and ω×OC=0 (parallel vectors), we get ω×r=ω×CP — a vector of magnitude ωr⊥​, tangential to the circle at P. This confirms ∣v∣=ωr⊥​, matching Eq. (6.19).

τ=r×Fforce F

10.4 Solved Example (NCERT 6.12) — Flywheel and Cord

10.4

Example 6.12 (NCERT) — Flywheel and Cord ⭐⭐

Reveal answer

Flywheel (M = 20 kg, R = 20 cm), pulled by a 25 N cord. A cord of negligible mass is wound round the rim of the flywheel; a steady pull of 25 N is applied, and the flywheel is mounted on frictionless bearings.

(a) Angular acceleration:τ=FR=25×0.20=5.0N m.I=2MR2​=220(0.2)2​=0.4kg m².

α=Iτ​=0.45.0​=12.5 rad/s2​

(b) Work done unwinding 2 m of cord:W=F×d=25×2=50 J​.

(c) Kinetic energy gained(starting from rest): angular displacementθ=2 m/0.2 m=10rad. Usingω2=ω02​+2αθ=0+2(12.5)(10)=250(rad/s)2.

K=21​Iω2=21​(0.4)(250)=50 J​

(d) Comparison:the kinetic energy gained (50 J) exactly equals the work done by the pull (50 J) — no energy is lost, since the bearings are frictionless. This is the rotational work–energy theorem in action.

10.1 Torque and Angular Acceleration

From the work-energy route (or directly from Newton's 2nd Law applied to rotation):

τ=Iα​...(6.41)

This is the exact rotational analogue of F=ma: produces , exactly as force produces linear acceleration, with I playing the role of inertia.

Interactive — same torque, different I, very different response: exactly the same shape of relationship as §11.2's ω=L/I hyperbola, but now for dynamics rather than conservation. Hold τ fixed and drag I: a small I (a light disc) snaps into fast rotation; a large I (a heavy ) barely budges under the same push. This is the entire reason a flywheel resists jerky speed changes (§8.8) — not a separate fact, but this exact curve.

Drag I down toward 0.5 and the angular acceleration T/I spikes; drag it up toward 8 and it barely registers — the same fixed torque, wildly different outcomes, purely because of how the mass is distributed.

If the Earth's volume suddenly shrinks to 1/64 of its original value (mass unchanged), find the new duration of the day.

11.3

Step 1 — find the new radius.SinceV∝R3:

Reveal answer

V′=64V​⇒34​πR′3=641​⋅34​πR3⇒R′=4R​

Step 2 — no external torque acts during the shrink(it's an internal redistribution of the Earth's own mass), so angular momentum is conserved. Treating Earth as a uniform solid sphere,I=52​MR2, andω=2π/T:

Iω=I′ω′⇒52​MR2⋅T2π​=52​MR′2⋅T′2π​

Step 3 — mass and the52​⋅2πfactors cancel, leaving:

TR2​=T′R′2​⇒T′=T(RR′​)2=T⋅161​

T′=1624​=1.5 hours​

A day would last just 1.5 hours — the Earth would spinsixteen times faster, purely because it got smaller while keeping the same mass and angular momentum.

11.2 Conservation of Angular Momentum

If I is allowed to change (mass redistributes relative to the axis) but τext​=0:

Lz​=Iω=constant​...(6.44)

So if I decreases, ω must increase to keep Iω fixed, and vice versa — this is the single most powerful idea in the chapter for solving "sudden change in shape/configuration" problems.

Turn this into a dial you can actually drag: with L held fixed, ω and I trace out the hyperbola ω=L/I below — pull Inow​ toward zero (arms tucked in tight) and watch ωnow​ shoot upward, exactly the "arms in → spin faster" effect in the panel above, now with numbers attached.

Watch K=L2/(2I) climb as you drag I down — this is the "kinetic energy increases" claim below, made concrete: halving I doesn't just double K, it quadruples it, because K∝1/I while ω∝1/I too.

A skater (or a person on a frictionless swivel chair) pulls their arms in: I decreases sharply, so ω increases to conserve L=Iω. Pulling arms back out reverses the effect. The kinetic energy K=21​Iω2=21​Lω actually increases when arms are pulled in (since ω increases while L stays fixed) — that extra energy comes from the muscular work done pulling the arms inward against the effective outward pull, not from nowhere.

Chapter Brief

This chapter extends particle mechanics to systems and rigid bodies, using the centre of mass to describe translation and torque and angular momentum to describe rotation. Moment of inertia connects rotational motion to its linear analogue, while equilibrium and conservation laws provide tools for solving rigid-body problems. The chapter is restricted to fixed-axis rotation (or angular momentum about a symmetry axis); general three-dimensional rotation and precession are outside its scope, and rolling motion is only previewed.

1.1

Summary

A is an ideal model that lets us study an extended object’s motion without tracking changes in its shape.

Important Notes

  • Rigid body — perfectly definite, unchanging shape; distance between every pair of particles stays constant under any force.
  • No real body is truly rigid — deformation often negligible in practice.

1.2

Summary

Translation carries all points together, rotation gives points different linear speeds at a shared angular speed, and rolling combines both motions.

Important Notes

  • **** — every particle has the same velocity at every instant. Example: block sliding down an incline.
  • **** — body rotates about a fixed axis; particles move in circles. Example: ceiling fan, potter’s wheel.
  • **** — translation + rotation combined. Example: cylinder rolling down an incline.
  • Pure translation → identical velocity for every particle.
  • Pure rotation about a fixed axis → identical ω for every particle; linear speeds still differ with radius.

1.3

Summary

In , each particle follows a circle centered on the axis, while points on the axis do not move.

Important Notes

  • Every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, centred on the axis.
  • Particle at perpendicular distance r from the axis traces a circle of radius r.
  • Particles on the axis: r=0⇒v=ωr=0 — stationary.
  • Axis of a spinning top is not fixed — it precesses. This chapter treats fixed-axis rotation only.

1.4

Summary

The common angular speed produces a linear speed proportional to each point’s distance from the axis.

Important Notes

  • vi​=ωri​ — Eq. (6.19).
  • Same ω for every point of a rotating body; linear speed scales linearly with radius from the axis.

2.1

Summary

The is the mass-weighted representative point whose translation captures the motion of the whole system under external forces.

Important Notes

  • COM — point that moves exactly as a single particle carrying the total mass M would move under the same external force.
  • Trap: COM coincides with the geometric centre only for uniform, symmetric bodies — not in general.

2.2

Summary

For two particles, the lies at their position average weighted by their masses.

Important Notes

  • xcm​=m1​+m2​m1​x1​+m2​x2​​ — Eq. (6.1).
  • Equal masses (m1​=m2​): xcm​=2x1​+x2​​ — midpoint.
  • xcm​ is the mass-weighted mean — pulled toward the heavier particle.

2.3

Summary

The two-particle rule extends to any number of particles by averaging each coordinate with the system’s mass distribution.

Important Notes

  • X=M∑mi​xi​​, similarly for Y, Z — Eq. (6.4a–c).
  • Vector form: R=M∑mi​ri​​ — Eq. (6.4d).
  • Origin chosen at the ⇒∑mi​ri​=0.

2.4

Summary

For a continuous body, the discrete weighted average becomes an integral over its mass elements.

Important Notes

  • X=M1​∫xdm, similarly for Y,Z — Eq. (6.5a).
  • Uniform symmetric body: = geometric centre. Every element dm at r is matched by an element at −r.

2.5

Summary

Symmetry identifies the for regular uniform bodies; composite or irregular shapes require combining the centres of their parts.

Important Notes

  • Body — COM
  • Uniform rod — Midpoint
  • Uniform ring — Centre
  • Uniform disc — Centre
  • Uniform sphere — Centre
  • Uniform triangular lamina —
  • -shaped lamina (uniform) — Mass-weighted average of sub-shapes
  • Trap: COM can lie outside the body’s material — ring, hollow sphere.

2.6

Summary

The examples apply weighted averages and symmetry to locate the of point-mass and extended-body systems.

Important Notes

  • Example 6.1 — 3 unequal masses (100 g, 150 g, 200 g) at triangle vertices: X=5/18 m, Y=1/(33​) m.
  • Example 6.2 — uniform triangular lamina: COM = , proved via the strip method (every strip’s midpoint lies on a median).
  • Example 6.3 — -lamina (3 kg, three 1 kg unit squares): COM at (5/6,5/6) m.

3.1

Summary

Internal forces cancel in the system total, so only external force determines the centre-of-mass acceleration.

Important Notes

  • MV=∑mi​vi​ — Eq. (6.8), velocity of .
  • MA=∑mi​ai​ — Eq. (6.9), acceleration of COM.
  • Each particle’s force Fi​ includes both external and internal contributions.
  • Internal action–reaction pairs cancel exactly on summing (Newton’s third law).
  • MA=Fext​ — Eq. (6.11): COM moves as if all mass were concentrated there and all external force applied there. True for any system, rigid or not.
  • Trap: internal forces (e.g. a mid-air explosion) never change the COM’s path — only external force (gravity) does.

3.2

Summary

Internal rearrangements can change how parts move relative to one another without changing the system’s centre-of-mass motion.

Important Notes

  • Radioactive decay: at rest before decay stays at rest — decay products fly apart back-to-back.
  • Binary stars: COM moves like a free particle. In the COM frame, the two stars orbit the COM, always diametrically opposite.
  • Problem-solving split: COM translation (external forces only) + motion relative to COM (internal dynamics).

4.1

Summary

The provides the vector operation needed to express and .

Important Notes

  • Torque and angular momentum are both defined via the cross product.

4.2

Summary

The combines a magnitude set by the perpendicular geometry with a direction normal to the two input vectors.

Important Notes

  • c=a×b: magnitude absinθ; direction ⟂ to the plane of a,b; sense by right-hand screw rule.

4.3

Summary

Cross-product order and grouping matter, while distributivity and the zero self-product support algebraic simplification.

Important Notes

  • Property — Statement
  • Not commutative — a×b=−b×a
  • Not associative — Order and grouping matter
  • Distributive — a×(b+c)=a×b+a×c
  • Self — a×a=0
  • Under reflection — Does not change sign (unlike polar vectors)

4.4

Summary

The cyclic order of the Cartesian unit vectors fixes the positive direction of their cross products.

Important Notes

  • ^×^=^​×^​=k^×k^=0.
  • ^×^​=k^, ^​×k^=^, k^×^=^​ — cyclic order → positive.
  • Reversed order → negative: ^​×^=−k^, k^×^​=−^, ^×k^=−^​.

4.5

Summary

The determinant expansion converts a vector into three signed component calculations.

Important Notes

  • a×b=(ay​bz​−az​by​)^+(az​bx​−ax​bz​)^​+(ax​by​−ay​bx​)k^.
  • Example 6.4 — a=3^−4^​+5k^, b=−2^+^​+3k^: a⋅b=5; a×b=−17^−19^​−5k^.

4.6

Summary

Dot and cross products encode different geometric outcomes: a scalar projection versus a perpendicular vector.

Important Notes

  • — Dot Product —
  • Result — Scalar — Vector
  • Formula — abcosθ — absinθ, direction ⟂ plane
  • Commutative — Yes — No
  • Zero when — θ=90° — θ=0° or 180°
  • Examples — Work, Power — ,

5.1

Summary

describes the rate and direction of rotation and connects directly to each point’s linear velocity.

Important Notes

  • ω=dθ/dt; SI rad s⁻¹; [T−1].
  • vi​=ωri​ — Eq. (6.19); same ω for every particle of the body.
  • Vector form v=ω×r — Eq. (6.20), valid even for rotation about a single fixed point.
  • Four rotational cross-products: v=ω×r (velocity); at​=α×r (tangential accel); L=r×p (, analogue of p=mv); τ=r×F (, analogue of F).

5.2

Summary

measures how changes; for fixed-axis motion its direction is fixed and its magnitude follows the scalar relation.

Important Notes

  • α=dω/dt, scalar form α=dω/dt — Eq. (6.21)/(6.22); SI rad s⁻²; [T−2].
  • : ω’s direction never changes — only magnitude.
  • α is therefore also fixed in direction for fixed-axis rotation — the vector equation collapses to the scalar one.

5.3

Summary

Circular motion has separate acceleration components: tangential acceleration changes speed, while centripetal acceleration continually changes direction.

Important Notes

  • at​=α×r, ∣at​∣=αr⊥​ — tangential acceleration, changes speed along the circle.
  • ac​=ω2r⊥​=v2/r⊥​ — centripetal acceleration, always toward the axis, changes direction only.
  • at​ vs ω: straight line, independent of ω. ac​ vs ω: parabola, ∝ω2.
  • Trap: α=0 (no ) does not mean zero acceleration — ac​=ω2r⊥​=0 persists as long as the particle keeps moving in a circle.

5.4

Summary

The cross-product relations show that and are genuine vectors, not merely scalar labels.

Important Notes

  • ω and α act as genuine 3-D vectors along the rotation axis, confirmed by both v=ω×r and at​=α×r computed as real cross products, not just plugged-in formulas.

6.1

Summary

measures how effectively a force tends to rotate a body about a chosen origin, depending on both its arm and direction.

Important Notes

  • τ=r×F — Eq. (6.23); SI N m; [ML2T−2] — same dimension as energy, but torque is a vector and energy a scalar.
  • τ=rFsinθ=rF⊥​=r⊥​F — Eq. (6.24a–c).
  • τ=0 if r=0, F=0, or the line of action of F passes through the origin (θ=0° or 180°).
  • Reverse F alone → τ reverses.
  • Reverse both r and F → τ unchanged.
  • τ=rFsinθ peaks at θ=90° (force ⟂ to r) — most effective angle; zero at θ=0°,180°.
  • Trap: τ=r⊥​F=rF⊥​ are equivalent — use whichever is more convenient for the geometry.

6.2

Summary

measures a particle’s rotational motion about an origin and changes when a acts.

Important Notes

  • L=r×p — Eq. (6.25a); SI kg m² s⁻¹ (= J s); [ML2T−1].
  • L=rpsinθ=rp⊥​=r⊥​p — Eq. (6.26a,b).
  • dL/dt=τ — Eq. (6.27), single particle. Exact rotational analogue of F=dp/dt.

6.3

Summary

For a system, internal torques cancel only under the stated force-pair conditions, leaving external to govern total .

Important Notes

  • System: L=∑li​=∑ri​×pi​ — Eq. (6.25b).
  • dL/dt=Στi​=τext​+τint​ — Eq. (6.28a).
  • Trap: τint​=0 needs two conditions together — Newton’s third law (equal & opposite) and the forces being collinear (central forces). Either alone is not enough.
  • With both conditions: dL/dt=τext​ — Eq. (6.28b).
  • τext​=0⇒L= constant — Eq. (6.29a), conservation of angular momentum.

6.4

Summary

The examples use the cross-product definition directly and differentiate when the momentum varies with time.

Important Notes

  • Example 6.5 — r=^−^​+k^, F=7^+3^​−5k^ → τ=2^+12^​+10k^ N m.
  • Example 6.6 — particle moving at constant v: angular momentum about any fixed point O stays constant. Perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion is fixed; consistent with zero on a free particle.
  • Method — torque from a time-varying momentum: build L(t)=r×p(t), then differentiate component-wise to get τ(t)=dL/dt.

7.1

Summary

A is in equilibrium only when both its net force and net vanish.

Important Notes

  • Mechanical equilibrium: ∑Fi​=0 (translational) — Eq. (6.30a); ∑τi​=0 (rotational) — Eq. (6.30b).
  • condition is independent of the origin chosen, provided also holds.

7.2

Summary

Force balance and balance are independent, so satisfying one condition does not guarantee full .

Important Notes

  • Rotational only, not translational: two equal parallel forces, same direction, at a rod’s two ends. Moments about the midpoint cancel; net force =2F=0.
  • Translational only, not rotational: reverse one of those forces. Net force =0; the pair now forms a — , no translation.

7.3

Summary

A produces because its equal and opposite forces cancel translationally while retaining a moment.

Important Notes

  • Couple — equal magnitude, opposite direction, different (parallel) lines of action; produces rotation with no translation.
  • of a couple =AB×F — independent of the origin chosen (a distinguishing feature).
  • Examples of couples: turning a bottle cap, a compass needle in Earth’s magnetic field.
  • Trap: a couple has zero net force but non-zero torque — translational and are independent conditions.

7.4

Summary

The balances opposing moments about its , allowing a longer effort arm to trade distance for force.

Important Notes

  • Lever — load F1​ at load arm d1​; effort F2​ at effort arm d2​; pivot at the fulcrum.
  • of a lever: R−F1​−F2​=0.
  • about the fulcrum: d1​F1​=d2​F2​ — Eq. (6.32a).
  • : M.A.=F1​/F2​=d2​/d1​ — Eq. (6.32b). d2​>d1​⇒M.A.>1: small effort lifts large load.
  • Lever examples: seesaw, beam balance, scissors, human forearm, pliers, crowbar.

7.5

Summary

The is the effective point of action of a body’s total gravitational and coincides with its in a uniform field.

Important Notes

  • Centre of Gravity (CG) — point where total gravitational torque is zero: ∑ri​×mi​g=0 — Eq. (6.33).
  • g uniform across the body ⇒ CG = COM (always true in this course).
  • Finding CG experimentally: suspend the body from a point, drop a plumb line; repeat from a second point; the intersection locates the CG.

7.6

Summary

The examples solve rigid-body by combining force balance with moments about a carefully chosen pivot.

Important Notes

  • Example 6.8 — bar (70 cm, 4 kg) on two knife edges with a 6 kg load: R1​≈54.88 N, R2​≈43.12 N.
  • Example 6.9 — ladder (3 m, 20 kg) against a frictionless wall, foot 1 m from the wall: N=196 N, F1​≈34.6 N (wall), floor friction ≈34.6 N, net floor force ≈199.0 N at ≈80° to horizontal.

8.1

Summary

measures rotational resistance by weighting each mass element according to its squared distance from the chosen axis.

Important Notes

  • I=∑mi​ri2​ — Eq. (6.34); ri​ = perpendicular distance from the axis. SI kg m²; [ML2].
  • I depends on mass, its distribution, and the axis chosen — unlike mass, I is not a fixed property of a body.
  • I weights distance heavily (r2 factor) — a small mass far from the axis can out-contribute a large mass close to it.

8.2

Summary

is the sum of particle kinetic energies and takes the translational form with I and ω in place of mass and speed.

Important Notes

  • Krot​=21​Iω2 — Eq. (6.35), derived from summing 21​mi​vi2​ with vi​=ri​ω.
  • I is the rotational analogue of mass; ω of v.

8.3

Summary

The represents a distributed body by an equivalent distance at which its full mass produces the same .

Important Notes

  • Radius of gyration k — distance at which the entire mass, concentrated as a point, reproduces the same I; RMS distance of all particles from the axis.
  • I=Mk2⇒k=I/M​. SI m; [L].
  • Body / Axis — k
  • Thin rod, midpoint — L/12​
  • Ring, central axis — R
  • Disc, central axis — R/2​
  • Disc, diameter — R/2
  • Solid sphere, diameter — R2/5​

8.4

Summary

Standard shapes have reusable moments of inertia, but every value is tied to a specified axis.

Important Notes

  • Body — Axis — I
  • Thin ring, radius R — ⟂ to plane, centre — MR2
  • Thin ring, radius R — Diameter — MR2/2
  • Thin rod, length L — ⟂, midpoint — ML2/12
  • Thin rod, length L — ⟂, one end (via §8.6) — ML2/3
  • Disc, radius R — ⟂ to disc, centre — MR2/2
  • Disc, radius R — Diameter — MR2/4
  • Hollow cylinder, radius R — Axis of cylinder — MR2
  • Solid cylinder, radius R — Axis of cylinder — MR2/2
  • Solid sphere, radius R — Diameter — 2MR2/5
  • Trap: hollow cylinder = ring (MR2); solid cylinder = disc (MR2/2); solid sphere =2MR2/5. Always specify the axis — the same body has a different I per row above.

8.4.1

Summary

Changing the axis changes the perpendicular distances of the body’s mass and therefore changes its .

Important Notes

  • The same body gives a different I for each different axis — Table 6.1’s rod, ring, and disc rows each list two axes for exactly this reason.

8.5

Summary

These derivations show how particle-level kinetic energy and a symmetric mass arrangement yield useful inertia results.

Important Notes

  • Thin ring about its own axis: all mass at distance R⇒I=MR2, via comparing K=21​Mv2 with K=21​Iω2.
  • Massless rod, point masses M/2 at each end, axis ⟂ through centre: I=Ml2/4.

8.6

Summary

The parallel-axis theorem shifts a known centre-of-mass inertia to a parallel axis by adding the mass-distance contribution.

Important Notes

  • I′=Icm​+Md2 — for any and any pair of parallel axes, d = perpendicular distance between them.
  • Doubling d quadruples the Md2 term — quadratic growth, not linear.
  • Worked: rod about one end — Iend​=12ML2​+M(2L​)2=3ML2​.

8.7

Summary

For a planar body, this theorem relates inertia about the normal axis to the two in-plane axes through the same point.

Important Notes

  • Iz​=Ix​+Iy​ — planar (laminar) bodies only, three mutually ⟂ axes meeting at one point.
  • Trap: does not apply to 3-D solids (sphere, solid cylinder) — planar bodies only.
  • Worked: disc about a diameter from disc about centre — Iz​=MR2/2, Ix​=Iy​ by symmetry ⇒Ix​=Iz​/2=MR2/4.
  • Worked: ring about a diameter — Iz​=MR2⇒Ix​=Iy​=MR2/2.

8.8

Summary

A 's large resists rapid changes in angular speed and smooths a machine’s rotation.

Important Notes

  • Flywheel — heavy disc, large I, used in engines. Resists sudden changes in angular speed, giving smooth motion despite fluctuating driving .

9.1

Summary

Constant produces rotational kinematics equations parallel to the constant-acceleration equations for linear motion.

Important Notes

  • ω=ω0​+αt — Eq. (6.36).
  • θ=θ0​+ω0​t+21​αt2 — Eq. (6.37).
  • ω2=ω02​+2α(θ−θ0​) — Eq. (6.38).
  • Valid only when angular acceleration α is constant.

9.2

Summary

Integrating constant first gives , then integrating velocity gives .

Important Notes

  • α=dω/dt= const → integrate → ω=ω0​+αt.
  • Integrate again → θ=θ0​+ω0​t+21​αt2.
  • rpm → rad/s: ω=30πN​.

9.3

Summary

The motor-wheel example applies constant-acceleration equations to infer both and total rotation.

Important Notes

  • Motor wheel, 1200 → 3120 rpm in 16 s: α=4π rad s⁻².
  • θ=1152π rad → 576 revolutions.

9.4

Summary

Uniform circular motion lets the minute hand’s angular speed be found directly from its period.

Important Notes

  • Minute hand: one revolution in 3600 s. ω=2π/3600≈1.745×10−3 rad/s.

9.5

Summary

Wheel stopping data can be converted into angular kinematics to determine its constant retardation.

Important Notes

  • Car wheel (72 km/h, diameter 0.5 m) stops in 20 rotations: angular retardation =80/π≈25.5 rad/s².

9.6

Summary

Rotational kinematics describes how θ, ω, and α evolve, while vector acceleration resolves the resulting motion into tangential and radial parts.

Important Notes

  • Tangential/centripetal decomposition (§5.3) combines with the θ,ω,α kinematics of §9.1 in one unified vector picture of circular motion.

10.1

Summary

For fixed-axis motion, changes in proportion to the body’s rotational inertia.

Important Notes

  • τ=Iα — Eq. (6.41), the rotational analogue of F=ma; I plays the role of inertia.
  • Fixed τ, small I (light disc) → large α, fast response.
  • Fixed τ, large I (heavy ) → small α, sluggish response — the mechanism behind a flywheel resisting jerky speed changes (§8.8).

10.2

Summary

transfers energy through , and its rate of doing work is rotational power.

Important Notes

  • dW=τdθ — Eq. (6.39).
  • P=τω — Eq. (6.40).

10.3

Summary

Linear and rotational dynamics share parallel roles for displacement, velocity, acceleration, inertia, force, and energy.

Important Notes

  • Linear — Rotational
  • Displacement x — θ
  • Velocity v=dx/dt — ω=dθ/dt
  • Acceleration a=dv/dt — α=dω/dt
  • Mass M — I
  • Force F=Ma — τ=Iα
  • Work dW=Fds — Work dW=τdθ
  • KE =Mv2/2 — KE =Iω2/2
  • Power P=Fv — Power P=τω
  • Momentum p=Mv — L=Iω

10.4

Summary

The example links applied to and checks the result by equating work with the kinetic-energy gain.

Important Notes

  • Flywheel (M=20 kg, R=20 cm), cord pulled with F=25 N: τ=FR=5.0 N m; I=MR2/2=0.4 kg m²; α=τ/I=12.5 rad/s².
  • 2 m of cord unwound: W=F×d=50 J; θ=d/R=10 rad; ω2=2αθ=250(rad/s)2; K=21​Iω2=50 J.
  • Work done equals kinetic energy gained (50 J = 50 J), frictionless bearings — confirms the rotational work–energy theorem.

11.1

Summary

The scalar relation Lz​=Iω is useful for when the body’s symmetry makes parallel to .

Important Notes

  • L=Iω — Eq. (6.42d), valid for a body symmetric about the rotation axis (true for every body in Table 6.1).
  • dtd​(Iω)=τext​; if I is constant this reduces to τ=Iα — Eq. (6.41).
  • Trap: L and ω are not always parallel — for a body not symmetric about its rotation axis, L=Iω (as vectors) is a special-case convenience, not a universal law.

11.2

Summary

With zero external , a change in rotational inertia is compensated by angular speed so that stays constant.

Important Notes

  • τext​=0, I allowed to change ⇒Lz​=Iω= constant — Eq. (6.44).
  • I decreases ⇒ω increases, and vice versa.
  • Skater: arms pulled in → I decreases sharply → ω increases to conserve L.
  • Kinetic energy K=21​Iω2=21​Lω increases when arms are pulled in. Extra energy comes from muscular work done pulling the arms in, not from nowhere.
  • K∝1/I while ω∝1/I too — halving I quadruples K, not just doubles it.

11.3

Summary

If Earth’s mass stays fixed and its radius shrinks without external , conservation of predicts a shorter rotation period.

Important Notes

  • Earth shrinks to 1/64 its volume, mass unchanged: V∝R3⇒R′=R/4.
  • No external torque during the shrink ⇒L conserved.
  • Treating Earth as a uniform solid sphere (I=52​MR2): R2/T=R′2/T′⇒T′=T/16=1.5 hours.
